persona.note: I have been trying to build apps on the side for years now and none of them have really worked. I keep going but I don't know what I am doing wrong anymore. I have a job, kids, my parents to look after, and this thing I keep failing at.

understanding.emotion: tired of trying and not sure why
understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call stuck and not starting, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from being stuck in years of unexplained failure to seeing what the failure has been teaching you and taking one step that is yours.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the exhaustion of years of trying that have not worked.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the doubt is not the problem. The unexamined effort is.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the years have not been wasted, and that the one who keeps pushing down becomes their own enemy.
week_beats.act: You try one act of stopping and learning from the failure, then one small step forward.
week_beats.story: A man who spent years building and failing shows you what it looks like to stop, see the lesson, and begin again.

understanding.core_struggle: A man with a job, children, and aging parents is trying to build apps on the side for years, but nothing has worked and he no longer knows what he is doing wrong.
understanding.mirror: You keep going, and the silence of the result is louder than the years of trying.
understanding.insight: It isn't that you are doing it wrong. It is that the path has become unclear, and the years of trying have made the doubt feel like proof.

queries.hook: The quiet ache of years of trying that have not worked, and the exhaustion of not knowing what is missing.
queries.diagnose: Doubt and delay feed each other; waiting to feel ready keeps us stuck, and the unexamined effort weighs more than the work itself.
queries.steady: The one who keeps pushing themselves down becomes their own enemy; lift yourself up and learn what this has been teaching you.
queries.act: Stop and write down one thing you have learned from each failed attempt, then choose one small step that is yours to take tomorrow.
queries.story: A man who has spent years building and failing, and who, when he finally stops, finds the first true step he was missing all along.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् । अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
verse.line: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.
verse.translation: I see nothing that could drive away this sorrow that is drying up my senses, not even an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth or rule over the gods.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna sits on the battlefield, the armies waiting, and tells Krishna that even a kingdom or the rule of gods would not lift the grief that is drying him up inside. He is tired of trying to see a way forward on his own. He admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him. The verse proposes that clarity begins when you stop pretending you know and ask for help.
verse.for_you: The years of building apps without a result have left you with a grief that no success could touch. You do not need to name the mistake or fix the failure right now.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: सर्वेषां कर्मणां तात फले नित्यमनित्यता / अनित्यमिति जानन्तो न भवन्ति भवन्ति च अथ ये नैव कुर्वन्ति नैव जातु भवन्ति ते / ऐकगुण्यमनीहायामभावः कर्मणां फलम्
verse.line: Every result is uncertain. Some who try succeed and some don't. Those who never try never do.
verse.translation: The result of every action is uncertain. Knowing this, some people act and succeed, some do not. But those who never act never succeed at all.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She tells him that the result of any action is uncertain. Some who try succeed and some do not, but those who never try never do. She is saying that the outcome of your effort is never guaranteed, yet the only certainty is that inaction leads to no success at all.
verse.for_you: You have been acting for years, so you are not frozen. The doubt you feel is not the real issue, it is the unexamined effort. Let the years of building show you that you are still in the arena, even if the path forward is hidden.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse.sanskrit: पूर्वाभ्यासेन तेनैव ह्रियते ह्यवशोऽपि सः । जिज्ञासुरपि योगस्य शब्दब्रह्मातिवर्तते ॥
verse.line: Past practice carries you forward, even when you don't feel like it.
verse.translation: By that former practice he is carried on, even against his will. Even one who merely wishes to know yoga goes beyond the ritual word.
verse.why: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

prasang.title: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

verse.meaning: Arjuna asks what happens to someone who tries and fails. Krishna says that even when you do not want to, your past practice carries you forward. The effort you have already put in does not vanish. It becomes the ground you stand on next time, so you do not start from nothing.
verse.for_you: The years of building those apps have not disappeared. They are the ground you stand on now, even when the doubt feels like proof against you.

verse.speaker: Bhishma
verse.setting: Bhishma on his bed of arrows begins teaching Yudhishthira how to lead.
verse.sanskrit: विपन्ने च समारम्भे सन्तापं मा स्म वै कृथाः / घटेतैवं सदाऽऽत्मानं राज्ञामेष परो नयः
verse.line: When something you started fails, don't torment yourself. Gather yourself and apply yourself again.
verse.translation: If an undertaking fails, do not torment yourself over it. Keep applying yourself again and again; this is the highest rule for those who lead.

matched.label: I can't tell if continuing is discipline or stubbornness

verse.meaning: Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, tells Yudhishthira that when a task fails, the leader should not torment themselves. The old practice of trying again carries them forward. The highest rule is to gather yourself and apply yourself once more, without letting the failure break your spirit.
verse.for_you: You have been building these apps for years. The failure of each one does not mean you could torment yourself. Gather your thoughts and apply yourself again, knowing that the practice itself is what carries you forward.

verse.speaker: Hanuman
verse.setting: Having searched all of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman fights off despair.
verse.sanskrit: अनिर्वेदः श्रियो मूलमनिर्वेदः परं सुखम्। भूयस्तत्र विचेष्यामि न यत्र विचयः कृतः॥
verse.line: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success. Look again where you have not yet looked.
verse.translation: Not losing heart is the root of success; not losing heart is the highest happiness. I will search again, in the places I have not yet searched.
verse.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

prasang.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
prasang.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasang.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
prasang.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

verse.meaning: Hanuman has searched all of Lanka through the night and cannot find Sita. He is close to despair, thinking of the shame and harm his failure will bring to Rama and the others. Then he speaks to himself, refusing to let his heart break. He says that refusing to lose heart is the root of success and the highest happiness. He decides he will search again, in the places he has not yet searched.
verse.for_you: You have searched the same paths for years. The failure has become heavy, but the cost of stopping is heavier. Take one small step today. Open the project folder you have avoided. Look again where you have not yet looked.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse.sanskrit: यो यमर्थं प्रार्थयते तदर्थं चेहते क्रमात् । अवश्यं स तमाप्नोति न चेदर्धान्निवर्तते ॥
verse.line: Want it, work for it step by step, and you will get there, unless you quit halfway.
verse.translation: Whoever wants something and works for it step by step will surely get it, unless they turn back halfway.
verse.why: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.
verse.misuse: Effort shapes results, but not every outcome is yours to control; see 2.6.21.

prasang.title: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

verse.meaning: Vasishtha sits with Rama, who is heavy with despair, and tells him that the future is not sealed by what has already happened. The teacher says that what people call fate is only the harvest of their own past actions, and that a stronger will can change the field. He tells the young prince to stop grieving over what was never truly in his hands, and to steer his own habits with care, as one raises a child.
verse.for_you: The years of apps are not a verdict on your ability. They are simply the soil your present effort will grow from. Choose one small action for today, and let the next step be enough.

story.title: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
story.story_hook: Bali had conquered everything there was to conquer, and one evening he realised he was bored.
story.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
story.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

anchor.speaker: Virochana
anchor.setting: Bali's father Virochana tells him the secret of mastering the mind.
anchor.sanskrit: एषा ह्यत्यन्तदुष्प्रापा सुप्रापा च महामते । अनभ्यस्तातिदुष्प्रापा स्वभ्यस्ता प्राप्यते सुखम् ॥
anchor.line: Unpractised, it feels impossible. Well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.translation: This is extremely hard to attain and also easy, great-minded one: unpractised, it is very hard to reach; well practised, it comes easily.
anchor.why: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

story.hook_title: A demon king who had conquered everything realised one evening that he was bored
story.teaser: A demon king who had conquered everything realised one evening that he was bored
story.for_you: Bali ruled everything and still felt empty. Your apps have not worked, and you are tired. The lesson is not to build more, but to win the mind that keeps you running the same loop. Stop the work for a moment and ask what the mind is actually doing.

script: You are tired of trying without knowing why. You have kept building these apps in the small hours, hoping one would work, while the work day and the family evening take up the rest.
Arjuna sits on the battlefield between the two armies. He is in tears. The great war is waiting. Arjuna said:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्, अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्.
In plain words: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.

Arjuna sits on the battlefield, the armies waiting, and tells Krishna that even a kingdom or the rule of gods would not lift the grief that is drying him up inside. He is tired of trying to see a way forward on his own. He admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him. The verse proposes that clarity begins when you stop pretending you know and ask for help.

Take the side project off the list for today. Keep the app building for tomorrow. Today, just notice that you do not know, and let that be the whole truth. You do not need to name the mistake or fix the failure right now.
What would it feel like to simply admit the path is unclear?

depth.life: You keep opening your laptop to build your apps. You keep going to work, you keep caring for your parents, you keep raising your children. But inside, something has dried up. You are tired of trying and you do not know why.
depth.points: Arjuna stood on the battlefield and admitted he could not see a way out, not even with victory. The texts say that admitting you do not know and asking for help is where clarity begins. Your grief is not a sign that you have failed. It is the sign that you have been trying without a guide.
depth.practice: Write down one sentence about what you are actually grieving right now.
depth.question: What would it feel like to stop trying to fix the app for one day?
